title: Surface access for Heathrow expansion — who pays, who builds, and who’s in charge?
label: 15 September 2026 · Heathrow surface access
summary: Witnesses from Heathrow Southern Railway, National Highways, the Heathrow Area Transport Forum and Transport for London gave evidence on the government’s draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement (HENPS). They welcomed ambitions for more public transport but warned the draft is weaker than earlier plans: it drops the ‘no extra traffic’ ambition, lacks firm commitments, leaves funding unclear and does not name a public lead to get the necessary western and southern rail links built in time.

chapters.title: Opening — first impressions of the draft HENPS
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses welcome ambition on public transport but say the draft HENPS is weaker than the 2018 approach and lacks firm commitments and delivery plans.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at surface transport in the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, known as HENPS. Can you introduce yourselves and give a quick view on whether the new document provides a credible plan?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: I’m Steven Costello from Heathrow Southern Railway, promoting a privately financed rail link into Heathrow. I think the HENPS mentions our ideas but the rules in it are too soft.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: I’m Elliot from National Highways. The draft has useful ambition on surface access, but the promoters need to show much more detailed plans so we can judge deliverability and road impacts.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: I chair the local Heathrow Area Transport Forum, which brings stakeholders together. The draft has good aims—public transport first and the environment—but it lacks clarity on who does what and who pays.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: I’m Alex from TfL. Overall I’m worried: the draft is weaker than the 2018 national policy statement. It drops Heathrow’s previous ‘no extra traffic’ aspiration and uses softer words like 'may' instead of 'required'.

chapters.title: Mode share, parking and staff travel
chapters.takeaway: Targets for public transport use are unchanged but may be unachievable without extra rail; the draft also omits a workplace travel target for staff.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: The draft keeps the old targets—50% then 55% public transport—but we don’t see a firm evidence base for those numbers and they won’t stop a big rise in road trips.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Heathrow’s own figures say about 48.4% of trips are already by public transport and around half of people still use a vehicle (taxis, drop-offs, parking). To hit 50–55% needs serious new services.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: A point on trips: our modelling shows that in 2025, with 84.5 million passengers, there were about 165,000 vehicle trips a day to the airport—not counting staff. That shows the scale of surface demand.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: The 2018 plan had a staff mode-share target and a staff travel plan. The new draft doesn’t—do you think that’s a problem?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Yes. About 80,000 people work at Heathrow and that workforce will grow. There’s no staff travel target in the draft and that omission matters for recruitment, fairness and traffic.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Staff are a tough group to shift—many work night shifts and value cars—but getting staff onto buses, bikes and trains is crucial if you want fewer car trips overall.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: What about parking and drop-off charges—could raising those push people to public transport?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: Heathrow’s own past work suggests simply raising the terminal drop-off charge doesn’t move the dial much. Hypothecating (ring‑fencing) drop-off or parking income for public transport could help, but it’s complex.

chapters.title: Rail schemes — what’s needed and who leads
chapters.takeaway: Everyone agrees western and southern rail links are essential, but the draft doesn’t make them required or name a public lead, so delivery and timing are unclear.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: The HENPS asks for a ‘credible plan’ for rail upgrades. Steven, what does a credible plan look like to you?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: For us it’s the Heathrow Southern Railway: a short, mostly tunneled link that connects Heathrow with lines to the south and west. We’ve spent years engineering and costing it; it’s private-finance ready if the policy framework gives certainty.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: TfL agrees more rail is needed and that the draft’s wording is too weak. In 2017 there were DfT and Network Rail teams actively working on western and southern options; now there’s no clear public body leading them.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Timing matters. If rail isn’t in place early, people get used to driving and habits stick. You can’t wait till passenger numbers hit 116m or 130m before starting major rail works.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: Rail projects take many years: we estimate eight years from approval to open. The draft treats rail as something that 'may' happen; that won’t work for complex, interdependent schemes.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Is western rail still deliverable given changes to the airport masterplan and availability of land?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: Some old western proposals were abandoned for being expensive or too narrow in benefit. Our approach integrates west and south so the same infrastructure helps many journeys and reduces community impact.

chapters.title: Who pays — private finance, public money and hypothecation
chapters.takeaway: Promoters say they can bring private money if policy gives certainty; TfL and others warn public funding or revenue‑ringfencing will still be needed.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: What funding models work? Steven, you mentioned a Thames Tideway-style approach—what does that mean?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: Thames Tideway (the London sewer tunnel) used a private company with a government support package to make it investable. We’re proposing a similar 'support package'—not cash but guarantees or commitments—so private lenders will finance the railway.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: From TfL’s view, the airport’s current regulatory setup doesn’t suit the scale of new spending here. There’ll have to be some public money or wider hypothecation (ring‑fencing of specific revenues such as parking or drop-off fees) because not all benefits fall on Heathrow alone.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Public benefits spill beyond the airport: better rail helps local towns, boosts land values and raises business rates. Those wider gains are part of the case for public contributions.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: Is there a real risk taxpayers pick up overruns?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Yes—history shows airport contributions can be reduced under regulation and government may end up filling gaps. The draft says promoters must pay full costs, but the practical details need sharpening.

chapters.title: Road network, construction and disruption risks
chapters.takeaway: Road impacts are uncertain; highways bodies want detailed promoter modelling and sequencing because the M25/M4 are already congested and construction will be lengthy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Has anyone modelled whether extra airport trips would make the M25 or M4 grind to a halt? We know those roads are already busy.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: National Highways hasn’t signed off specific modelling yet—we need the promoters’ detailed numbers. We expect promoters to show where additional traffic goes and how they’ll create capacity or mitigate impacts.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Heathrow has bought transport modelling licences and work is under way, but we haven’t seen the results. Until we see that modelling we can’t say what the extra traffic will do to flow or safety.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Construction will be long and complex. Local people worry about buses, cycling, and junction works; sequencing to avoid simultaneous disruption on road and rail is vital.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: A practical point: building rail early helps construction material delivery and waste removal by train, reducing heavy lorry traffic. That’s another reason to bring rail forward, not leave it to the end.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: What about freight during construction and after—will the plan handle the extra servicing and delivery vehicles?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: Promoters must set out construction phasing and freight movement plans in their Development Consent Order (DCO). To be clear, a DCO is the planning decision for big infrastructure projects—like the runway or tunnel consents—and it should detail traffic and mitigation.

chapters.title: What needs to change before Parliament decides
chapters.takeaway: The panel wants clearer, stronger rules in HENPS: require western/southern rail, set staff travel targets, show funding routes, and name a public lead with enforceable sequencing and contingency.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If a promoter met the draft HENPS surface access conditions, would that be enough to avoid harming local and strategic transport networks?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Even if they hit the 50–55% mode share, that still means around 60,000 extra vehicle trips a day on local highways. The deletion of the 'no extra traffic' aspiration is significant and means you must be realistic about road impacts.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: We need more upfront detail: firm targets for staff travel, a clear public lead to drive rail schemes, and credible, sequenced construction plans so people aren’t hit by simultaneous big projects.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: For private promoters to invest we need an 'investable pathway' in the policy: stronger language that recognises western and southern rail as essential and mechanisms that give private finance certainty—without exposing the taxpayer.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: From a highways view we expect promoters to demonstrate there’s capacity for the trips they forecast, to set out phasing and mitigations, and to be clear about any road works needed on the strategic road network.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. In short: the ambitions are welcome but the plan must be firmer on the rail projects, funding and staff travel, and must require the detailed modelling and sequencing the highways and rail operators need to avoid large-scale disruption.
